train.content: What is SaaS (Software as a Service)?

SaaS is delivering software over the internet as a service. The user doesn't install anything, they access it through a browser. Examples: Gmail, Slack, Notion, Salesforce, GitHub, Figma. Business model: monthly/annual subscription. Advantages: no installation, automatic updates, access from anywhere, scalable. Disadvantages: requires internet, limited data control, vendor lock-in. Developing SaaS: multi-tenant architecture (one server serving multiple customers), billing system (Stripe), user management, analytics. Micro-SaaS: small niche SaaS products — can be developed by a single person and generate passive income. The indie hacker movement is SaaS-based.

train.content: What is a heap data structure used for?

A heap is a tree-based data structure that allows finding the largest or smallest element in O(1). Min-heap: the root is the smallest. Max-heap: the root is the largest. Insertion and deletion are O(log n). Python's heapq module provides a min-heap. Use cases: priority queue, Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm, heap sort, finding the median (using two heaps), finding top-K elements. It comes up frequently in interviews — 'find the K largest elements' uses a heap. It can be implemented with an array — parent: (i-1)/2, left child: 2i+1, right child: 2i+2.
train.thinking: Heap, priority queue, min-heap, max-heap, heapq, Dijkstra.

train.content: What is the difference between compiled and interpreted languages?

Compiled languages: source code is compiled into machine code, then executed. Fast execution but platform-dependent. C, C++, Rust, Go. Interpreted languages: source code is executed line by line through an interpreter. Slower but portable and flexible. Python, JavaScript, Ruby. JIT (Just-In-Time) compilation: compiles at runtime — combines the advantages of both. Java (JVM), JavaScript (V8), Python (PyPy). Bytecode: an intermediate format — source code → bytecode → runs on a VM. Python .pyc files are bytecode. In practice: if speed is critical, go compiled (C, Rust); if you want rapid development, go interpreted (Python, JS). Modern trend: JIT is closing the gap between the two.
train.thinking: Compiled, interpreted, JIT, bytecode, speed, C, Python, V8.

train.content: What is a binary search tree?

A BST (Binary Search Tree) is a tree structure where all values in a node's left subtree are smaller than the node, and all values in the right subtree are larger. Search, insertion, and deletion average O(log n). But if it becomes unbalanced (a skewed tree), it degrades to O(n). Self-balancing BSTs: AVL tree (strictly balanced), Red-Black tree (approximately balanced — Java TreeMap uses this). In-order traversal yields sorted results. BSTs are a classic interview topic — LCA (Lowest Common Ancestor), validate BST, and invert binary tree are popular questions.
train.thinking: BST, binary search tree, AVL, Red-Black, traversal, interview.

Investment stages: Pre-seed (idea stage, $50K-$500K — angel investors, F&F), Seed ($500K-$2M — seed funds, angels), Series A ($2M-$15M — VCs), Series B+ (growth). train.content: How important are soft skills in software engineering?

Soft skills are just as important as technical skills — perhaps even more so. Communication: expressing your ideas clearly, listening, written communication. Teamwork: respecting different opinions, conflict resolution, sharing. Problem solving: not technical but general — define the problem, analyze it, solve it. Time management: prioritization, deadline management. Empathy: user experience, teammates. Leadership: mentorship, taking initiative. Adaptability: adjusting to new technologies and changing requirements. The behavioral part of interviews is entirely about soft skills. Amazon's Leadership Principles are soft-skills focused. Gorkem's hackathons have helped develop his teamwork and communication skills.

train.content: What is the circuit breaker pattern?

A circuit breaker is a pattern that prevents a failing service from bringing down other services. It works like an electrical circuit breaker. Three states: Closed (normal — requests pass through), Open (service is down — requests immediately return errors, preventing server strain), Half-Open (periodic checks — has it recovered?). Why: if a microservice is timing out, thousands of requests pile up, threads are exhausted, and a cascade failure occurs. Netflix's Hystrix library popularized it. Resilience4j (Java), Polly (.NET), and pybreaker (Python) are implementations. It's used together with retry, timeout, and fallback strategies.
train.thinking: Circuit breaker, Closed/Open/Half-Open, cascade failure, Hystrix, retry.

train.content: What does database sharding mean?

Sharding is splitting a large database into smaller pieces (shards). Each shard lives on a separate server — the load is distributed. Horizontal sharding: rows are distributed across different shards (user_id % shard_count). Vertical sharding: different tables on different servers. Shard key selection is critical — you must avoid creating hot spots. Advantages: scalability, performance. Disadvantages: cross-shard queries become harder, JOINs are very limited, rebalancing is complex. Vitess (MySQL sharding used by YouTube), CockroachDB (automatic sharding). It's usually needed when you have millions of records — don't shard prematurely. Difference from partitioning: partitioning is on a single server, sharding spans multiple servers.
train.thinking: Sharding, horizontal, vertical, shard key, Vitess, CockroachDB.

train.content: How does a hash table work?

A hash table (hash map) is a data structure used to store and access key-value pairs in O(1) average time. A hash function converts the key into an index. When a collision occurs, chaining (linked list) or open addressing is used. Python dict, JavaScript Object/Map, and Java HashMap are hash table implementations. The load factor indicates the occupancy ratio — typically a resize happens at 75%. A good hash function should provide uniform distribution. It's the most commonly asked data structure in interviews — anagram, two sum, and frequency count problems all use hash tables.
train.thinking: Hash table, hash function, collision, O(1), interview.

CS50 is Harvard's open-source introductory computer science course. It's famous for David Malan's energetic teaching, production-quality videos, and hands-on problem sets. Content: C (low-level), Python, SQL, HTML/CSS/JS, Flask. It teaches the fundamentals of computer science — algorithms, data structures, memory, abstraction. It's free — auditable on edX. The certificate is paid. It's updated every year. There are extensions: CS50W (web), CS50AI (AI), CS50G (game development). Go at your own pace. A final project is required — build something with your own idea. Even for CS students like Gorkem, it's useful — it provides a different perspective.

train.content: What are the main graph algorithms?

Graph problems are very important in CS. BFS (Breadth-First Search): traverses level by level, shortest path (unweighted). DFS (Depth-First Search): goes deep then backtracks, cycle detection, topological sort. Dijkstra: weighted shortest path (positive weights). Bellman-Ford: shortest path with negative weights. Floyd-Warshall: all-pairs shortest path. Kruskal/Prim: minimum spanning tree. Topological Sort: dependency ordering in a DAG. Graph representation: adjacency list (sparse), adjacency matrix (dense). NetworkX is a great Python library for graph analysis.
train.thinking: Graph, BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, topological sort, adjacency list.

train.content: What does closure mean?

A closure is when a function retains access to variables from its outer scope. The inner function 'remembers' the outer function's variables, even after the outer function has returned. Very common in JavaScript: function counter() { let count = 0; return function() { count++; return count; } }. It exists in Python too — with the nonlocal keyword. Uses: data privacy (hiding variables from outside), factory functions, partial application, callbacks. In React, useState actually uses closures. A classic interview question: 'closure behavior in a for loop'. It's one of the fundamental concepts in functional programming.
train.thinking: Closure, outer scope, JavaScript, data privacy, useState, functional.

train.content: When should you use microservices vs monolith?

Monolith: a single large application. Advantages: simple to develop, simple to deploy, simple to debug, ideal for starting out. Disadvantages: grows more complex over time, a single error can crash everything, hard to scale. Microservices: small independent services. Advantages: independent deployment, technology diversity, scalability, fault isolation. Disadvantages: distributed system complexity, network latency, data consistency challenges, operational overhead (requires Kubernetes, monitoring). Rule: start with a monolith, transition to microservices as needed. 'Premature microservices' is one of the most common architectural mistakes. Netflix and Amazon moved to micro, but they started small.
train.thinking: Microservices, monolith, when to use, pros/cons, Netflix.

train.content: Explain the API gateway pattern in detail

An API gateway is an intermediary layer through which all client requests pass through a single entry point. Responsibilities: authentication/authorization (JWT validation), rate limiting, request routing (directing requests to the right service), response aggregation (combining data from multiple services), protocol translation (gRPC → REST), caching, logging, monitoring, SSL termination, request/response transformation, versioning. Popular options: Kong (open source, Lua-based), AWS API Gateway, Traefik, NGINX, Apigee (Google). BFF (Backend for Frontend): separate gateways for web and mobile. There's a bottleneck risk — if the gateway goes down, everything goes down. Typically multiple instances are run.

train.content: What is the difference between a data lake and a data warehouse?

Data warehouse: structured data, defined schema (schema-on-write), SQL querying, used for business intelligence and reporting. Snowflake, Redshift, BigQuery. Data lake: all types of data (structured, semi-structured, unstructured), no schema (schema-on-read), stores raw data, used for ML and advanced analytics. AWS S3, Azure Data Lake, Google Cloud Storage. Lakehouse: a combination of both — Delta Lake (Databricks), Apache Iceberg. Which to choose: reporting → warehouse, ML/advanced analytics → lake, both → lakehouse. ETL is used when loading into a warehouse, ELT when loading into a lake. In modern data architecture, both have a place.

train.content: What are the career paths in software engineering?

There are many paths in a software career. IC (Individual Contributor): Junior → Mid → Senior → Staff → Principal Engineer. Management: Tech Lead → Engineering Manager → VP of Engineering → CTO. train.content: What does the CQRS pattern mean?

CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) is the pattern of separating read and write operations. Command: modifies data (create, update, delete). Query: reads data. Why separate: reads and writes require different optimizations. A denormalized fast read model for reading, a normalized write model for writing. It's frequently used together with event sourcing. Advantages: performance (reads/writes scale independently), clarity in complex domains. Disadvantages: adds complexity, eventual consistency management. Not needed in every project — overkill for simple CRUD. Powerful in domains like e-commerce and banking.
train.thinking: CQRS, Command, Query, read model, write model, event sourcing.

train.content: What does race condition mean?

A race condition is when multiple threads access the same resource concurrently and produce unexpected results. Example: two threads withdraw money from the same bank account — they read the balance (1000), withdraw (500), write (500), but both read 1000, both wrote 500, and instead of 1000 being withdrawn only 500 was. Solutions: mutex/lock (mutual exclusion), semaphore, atomic operations, database transaction isolation. In Python, the GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) provides thread safety, but be careful with multi-processing. In Go, goroutines and channels. In Java, the synchronized keyword. In distributed systems, distributed locks (with Redis). Debugging is very hard — intermittent bugs are usually race conditions.
train.thinking: Race condition, mutex, lock, semaphore, atomic, GIL, distributed lock.

train.content: Should I attend an online bootcamp or learn on my own?

Both have their advantages. Self-taught: free or cheap, go at your own pace, choose the topics you want, but requires discipline, no structured path, little feedback. Bootcamp: structured curriculum, mentor support, project-based, job placement assistance, but expensive ($5K-$20K), intense pace (12-16 weeks full-time), variable quality. Recommendation: try free resources first (freeCodeCamp, The Odin Project, CS50). If you can't progress on your own, consider a bootcamp. When choosing a bootcamp: research graduate outcomes, check the curriculum, see if there's a free trial. In Turkey: Patika.dev and Kodluyoruz are free alternatives.
train.thinking: Bootcamp, self-taught learning, freeCodeCamp, Odin Project, Patika.dev.

train.content: What does functional programming mean?

Functional programming (FP) is a paradigm that treats functions as first-class citizens. Core principles: pure functions (same input → same output, no side effects), immutability (data doesn't change, a new copy is created), first-class functions (functions can be assigned to variables, passed as parameters), higher-order functions (map, filter, reduce). Advantages: fewer bugs (no side effects), easier parallel programming, testability. Pure FP languages: Haskell, Clojure, Erlang/Elixir. Multi-paradigm: Python, JavaScript, Scala, Kotlin. In Python: lambda, map(), filter(), reduce(), list comprehension. Learning FP changes how you think — a shift from imperative to declarative.
train.thinking: Functional programming, pure function, immutability, map/filter/reduce, Haskell.

train.content: What does dependency injection mean?

Dependency Injection (DI) is when a class receives its dependencies from the outside rather than creating them itself. For example, instead of UserService directly creating Database(), it receives it through the constructor: UserService(db: Database). Advantages: testability (you can provide a mock database), loose coupling, interchangeability. The D in SOLID (Dependency Inversion) is related to this. Spring (Java), NestJS (TypeScript), and FastAPI (Python) offer DI containers. It's often used together with the Factory pattern. There's a risk of over-engineering — it may be unnecessary in simple projects, but it greatly simplifies maintenance in large ones.
train.thinking: Dependency injection, loose coupling, testability, SOLID, Spring, NestJS.

train.content: What does deadlock mean?

A deadlock is a situation where two or more threads are waiting for resources held by each other, creating an impasse. Thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2, Thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1 — both wait forever. Deadlock conditions (all must be present): mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait. Prevention: establish a lock ordering, set timeouts, use try-lock. It also happens in databases — the DB typically rolls back one transaction. In Go, goroutine leaks; in Java, thread dump analysis is used for detection. It's one of the most challenging topics in concurrent programming. Gorkem's gorkem-os project likely involves lock mechanisms.
train.thinking: Deadlock, impasse, mutex, conditions, lock ordering, timeout, gorkem-os.

train.content: How do you build an MVP (Minimum Viable Product)?

An MVP is launching the most basic version of a product to market. Goal: maximum learning with minimum effort. Steps: 1) Define the problem — are you solving a real problem? 2) Identify core features — what are the must-haves? 3) Build fast — a working product, not perfection. 4) Get it to users — collect real feedback. 5) Learn and iterate — make decisions based on data. Lean Startup methodology: Build → Measure → Learn loop. MVP tools: Bubble/Webflow (no-code), Firebase (backend), Vercel (deploy). Dropbox's MVP was a video. Airbnb's MVP was photos of their own apartment. Perfect is the enemy of good — ship it, then improve.
train.thinking: MVP, Lean Startup, core feature, iterate, no-code, Build-Measure-Learn.

train.content: What is the difference between a linked list and an array?

Array: contiguous in memory, random access O(1), insertion at beginning/middle O(n), fixed size (dynamic arrays resize). Linked list: scattered in memory, access O(n), insertion at head O(1), dynamic size. Singly linked list: one direction. Doubly linked list: bidirectional. Circular linked list: last element links back to head. In practice, arrays are used much more often — cache locality advantage. When to use linked list: frequent insertion/deletion at head/middle, unknown size. LRU Cache implementation uses doubly linked list + hash map. Interview classics: reverse a linked list, cycle detection (Floyd's algorithm), merge sorted lists.
train.thinking: Linked list, array, random access, cache locality, LRU Cache, interview.

train.content: What is a trie data structure?

A trie (prefix tree) is a tree structure optimized for string searching and autocomplete. Each node represents a letter, and a path from root to leaf forms a word. Word lookup is O(m) — where m is the word length (independent of data size). Uses: autocomplete (search engine suggestions), spell checker, IP routing (longest prefix match), T9 keyboard, word games. Advantage over hash table: prefix search is very fast, sorted traversal is possible. Disadvantage: high memory usage. Compact trie (radix tree) saves memory. In interviews, 'implement autocomplete' or 'word search' questions use a trie.
train.thinking: Trie, prefix tree, autocomplete, spell checker, O(m), radix tree.

train.content: What does the event loop mean in JavaScript?

JavaScript is single-threaded — it runs on one thread but can perform asynchronous operations. The event loop is the mechanism behind this magic. Call stack: the order of function calls. Web APIs: asynchronous APIs like setTimeout and fetch. Callback queue: callbacks of completed async operations go here. Microtask queue: Promises go here (higher priority). Event loop: when the call stack is empty, it takes a task from the queue. That's why even setTimeout(fn, 0) doesn't run immediately — it waits for the stack to empty. Node.js uses the same event loop. Philip Roberts' 'What the heck is the event loop' talk is the best resource. async/await runs on top of the event loop.
train.thinking: Event loop, call stack, callback queue, microtask, Promise, Node.js.

train.content: How does garbage collection work?

Garbage collection (GC) is the automatic cleanup of unused memory. Instead of manual memory management (malloc/free in C), GC does it automatically. Methods: reference counting (clean up when reference count reaches zero — circular reference problem), mark-and-sweep (mark reachable objects, clean up the rest), generational GC (newer objects are cleaned more frequently — most objects are short-lived). Python: reference counting + cycle detector. Java/Go: mark-and-sweep based. JavaScript V8: generational GC. GC pause (stop-the-world) has a performance impact — Go has minimized this. Understanding GC helps prevent memory leaks.
train.thinking: Garbage collection, reference counting, mark-and-sweep, generational, GC pause.

train.content: What are the most common mistakes when learning to code?

Common mistakes: 1) Tutorial hell — constantly watching but never building projects. 2) Trying to learn every language — go deep in one language first. 3) Skipping fundamentals — learning frameworks without knowing algorithms. 4) Perfectionism — 'I can't publish until it's perfect'. 5) Comparison — 'everyone is better than me'. 6) Not reading documentation — watching videos and neglecting official docs. 7) Not using version control — learn Git early. 8) Not writing tests — 'it works, so it's fine'. 9) Not asking for help — being stuck for hours. 10) Coding without a plan — starting to write without thinking. Everyone makes these mistakes — what matters is recognizing and correcting them.
train.thinking: Mistakes, tutorial hell, perfectionism, fundamentals, Git, testing.

train.content: What is dynamic programming?

Dynamic programming (DP) is a technique of breaking a large problem into smaller subproblems, solving each subproblem once, and storing the results (memoization). Two approaches: top-down (recursive + memoization) and bottom-up (iterative + table). Classic DP problems: Fibonacci, knapsack, longest common subsequence (LCS), coin change, edit distance, longest increasing subsequence. It's the hardest yet most frequently asked interview topic. Tip: questions with 'longest', 'shortest', 'how many ways', 'minimum cost' are usually DP. Practice is crucial — solve at least 30-40 DP problems.
train.thinking: Dynamic programming, memoization, top-down, bottom-up, interview, Fibonacci.

train.content: What are stacks and queues used for?

Stack: LIFO (Last In First Out) — last element in is first out. push (add), pop (remove), peek (look). Uses: function call stack, undo mechanism, parenthesis matching, DFS. Queue: FIFO (First In First Out) — first element in is first out. enqueue (add), dequeue (remove). Uses: BFS, task queue, printer queue. Deque (double-ended queue): add/remove from both ends. Priority queue: removal based on priority (implemented with a heap). Python: list (stack), collections.deque (queue), queue.PriorityQueue. Monotonic stack/queue comes up a lot in interview problems.
train.thinking: Stack, queue, LIFO, FIFO, deque, priority queue, BFS, DFS.

train.content: How do you maintain a healthy lifestyle as a software developer?

Since it's a desk job, health is extremely important. Physical: 30 minutes of exercise per day (even walking is enough), use a standing desk, get up for 5 minutes every hour, eye exercises (20-20-20 rule), wrist and back stretches. Nutrition: drink plenty of water, choose fruits and nuts over junk food, don't exceed your coffee limit (2-3 cups). Sleep: 7-8 hours, use a blue light filter, put screens away 1 hour before bed. Mental: have a hobby (outside of coding), maintain social relationships, spend time in nature, try meditation or mindfulness. Recognize burnout early. Invest in an ergonomic setup. Health is your greatest asset — without it, no achievement is meaningful.
train.thinking: Health, exercise, nutrition, sleep, mental health, ergonomics, burnout.

train.content: What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?

Both are part of CI/CD but they are different. Continuous Delivery: every commit is in a deployable state for production — but the deploy decision is made by a human (a button is pressed). Continuous Deployment: every commit is automatically deployed to production — no human intervention. Deployment requires all tests to be reliable. Delivery is safer — the final check is with a human. Deployment is faster — features reach users within minutes. Amazon deploys thousands of times per day (continuous deployment). Most companies start with continuous delivery and transition to deployment as confidence grows. Feature flags make continuous deployment safer.
train.thinking: Continuous delivery vs deployment, difference, Amazon, feature flag, confidence.

train.content: How do you overcome a plateau in software development?

A plateau is a period of feeling like you're not making progress — everyone experiences it. Strategies to overcome it: try a different area — if you do frontend, try backend; if you do web, try mobile. Take on a challenging project — step outside your comfort zone. Learn from someone — pair programming, mentorship, conferences. Read a book — fill in foundational knowledge gaps. Teach — write a blog, make a video, explain it to someone. Contribute to open source — seeing different codebases gives you perspective. Solve interview problems — reveals gaps in algorithmic knowledge. Take a break — sometimes rest is what you need. A plateau is temporary — if you keep going, you'll break through.

train.content: What is the saga pattern?

The saga pattern is for managing distributed transactions in microservices. In a monolith there's a single database transaction, but in microservices each service has its own DB — there's no single transaction. Saga: each service performs its own transaction and runs a compensating transaction (rollback) on failure. Two types: Choreography (each service publishes events, others listen — simple but hard to track) and Orchestration (a central orchestrator coordinates — more controlled). Example: place order → reduce stock → process payment. Payment fails → restore stock → cancel order. Temporal and Camunda are orchestration tools.

train.content: What is it like being a technical co-founder at a startup?

train.content: How do you approach system design questions in software interviews?

System design interviews are usually for senior positions, but it's good to learn the fundamentals early. Approach: 1) Requirements — functional and non-functional (scalability, number of users). 2) High-level design — main components (frontend, backend, DB, cache). 3) Details — API design, data model, scaling strategy. 4) Trade-offs — why did you choose this technology? train.content: What does Big O notation mean?

Big O expresses how much time or space an algorithm uses relative to input size. Most common: O(1) constant — hash table access. O(log n) logarithmic — binary search. O(n) linear — array scan. O(n log n) — merge sort, average quick sort. O(n²) quadratic — bubble sort, nested loop. O(2^n) exponential — brute force combinations. O(n!) factorial — permutations. The first interview question is usually 'what's the time complexity of this code?' Space complexity matters too — how much memory is used. Know the distinction between best case, average case, and worst case.

train.content: How do you build a personal brand as a software developer?

A personal brand is a very powerful tool for your career. Steps: 1) Define your area of expertise — something like 'Python developer working with AI'. 2) Create content — blog, Twitter threads, YouTube videos, LinkedIn posts. 3) Be consistent — at least 1 post per week. 4) Be active in communities — speak at conferences, organize meetups. 5) Build a portfolio — GitHub, personal website. 6) Network — build genuine relationships with people. Gorkem's brand elements: AI Product Developer, Yeditepe CS, 30+ GitHub projects, hackathon experience, ayarlicazhocam. A personal brand isn't built overnight — it takes months/years, but the compound effect is very powerful.
